title: Agent-based model
summary: Agent-based modeling (ABM) is a computational simulation approach that represents a system as numerous autonomous agents interacting within a shared environment. Each agent follows simple decision-making rules or heuristics, and system-level patterns emerge from their simultaneous interactions. ABMs are used across biology, ecology, and social science to explore how micro-level behaviors generate macro-level outcomes. The approach originated in the late 1940s with theoretical machines, expanded through 1970s segregation and colony models, and saw major growth in the 1990s with large-scale simulations like Sugarscape. ABMs are typically implemented as computer simulations using custom software or toolkits to test how changes in individual behavior affect overall system dynamics.

mechanisms.title: Emergent pattern formation
mechanisms.explanation: System-level properties arise from the simultaneous interactions of many simple agents following local rules, without centralized control. Higher-level patterns such as aggregation, segregation, or cultural diffusion emerge from these bottom-up interactions.

mechanisms.title: Rule-based agent decision making
mechanisms.explanation: Individual agents are characterized as boundedly rational, acting according to perceived self-interest using heuristics or simple decision rules. Agents may also exhibit learning, adaptation, and reproduction within the simulation environment.
